title: Create a partitioned Icerberg Table from dbt using Athena Connector
answer:
Iceberg tables are stored in this way to optimize S3 performance. What you see in your screenshot is random prefixes that help spread out the table's data over a wider keyspace. It's a feature, not a bug. Consider Iceberg table storage opaque. It's managed by the Iceberg library, and everything is recorded in the manifests. Don't read out any significance from the locations of the files themselves.

Iceberg tables don't have primary keys. Primary keys are hard, and very expensive to enforce in a data lake setting, and it's also not something that analytics workloads need in general. The unique_key configuration in dbt is the closest thing you will have to a primary key. It basically tells dbt how to formulate updates so that the right row gets updated. You should probably not have the same unique_key as partition_by. If your rows have some kind of ID similar to what you would pick as a primary key in a relational database, use that as your unique_key.

I'm not sure you can tell dbt to delete data. If you want your model to represent a rolling window of time you may be better off using a regular model and recreate the table on every run.
